title: Mummadi Opens the Treasury of Knowledge

title_i18n.en: Mummadi Opens the Treasury of Knowledge

subtitle: How Mummadi Turned a Palace into a Living Library of Images
region: Mysore Palace, Jagan Mohan Palace and the Oriental Research Institute
moral: A court can preserve knowledge when it becomes a workshop.

sources.citation: Sritattvanidhi manuscript, Oriental Research Institute, University of Mysore
sources.note: Royal illuminated compendium attributed to Krishnaraja Wodeyar III.
Court chronicle produced under Wodeyar patronage and important for Mysore historical memory.

sources.citation: Norman Sjoman, The Yoga Tradition of the Mysore Palace (1996; rev. 1999)
sources.note: Modern study and translation of the Sritattvanidhi yoga material.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide inside a dim palace hall lined with manuscripts and paintings

dialogue.text: In a Mysore watched by Company officers and priests, Krishnaraja Wodeyar III built a different fortress — a palace where gods, games and yoga were painted, named and saved in the Sritattvanidhi.

panels.shot: slow push-in from balcony high above the Mysore Palace courtyard

dialogue.text: Restored as a child to a reduced throne, Krishnaraja Wodeyar III ruled under British supervision, between old ritual and new empire, searching for a space where his power could be his own.

panels.shot: medium interior shot at a writing desk lit by a single oil lamp

dialogue.text: Unlike warriors before him, Mummadi turned inward. The court became his workshop, his weapons ink and brush, his ambition to capture a kingdom of memory between covers.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up of a manuscript folio being opened

dialogue.text: From this urge was born the Sritattvanidhi, a grand Kannada compendium. Not a poem, not a single scripture, but a treasury where pictures and words marched together in disciplined rows.

panels.shot: bird's-eye view of a palace studio with multiple artists at work

dialogue.text: Mysore already had painters and priests. Mummadi gave them a manual. Each image in the Sritattvanidhi fixed posture, ornament and color, a reference for every artist in his kingdom.

panels.shot: tight close-up on a painter’s hand finishing an icon

dialogue.speaker: krishnaraja_wodeyar_iii
dialogue.text: The hand may change, but the form must stay true.
The compendium did not invent new gods; it disciplined their faces, weapons and moods, so that Mysore’s images followed one shared memory instead of many scattered habits.

panels.shot: medium shot of the king watching dancers and priests in a temple hall

dialogue.text: Outside the pages, ritual went on in halls and shrines. Inside the pages, he tried to catch its order — which god stood how, which symbol meant what, so that practice and painting could speak the same language.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of a quiet chamber with drawn yoga postures on the floor

dialogue.text: One section of the Sritattvanidhi went further. It pictured human bodies in yoga postures, joining older textual lists with the eye of a painter, making a bridge between practice, instruction and image.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of the king watching a court yogi hold a posture

dialogue.speaker: krishnaraja_wodeyar_iii
dialogue.text: The line must remember the body as it truly stands.
Later scholars would mine these drawings to trace Mysore’s yoga tradition, but in his own day they were part of the same urge — to see, to name, to file away for those yet to come.

panels.shot: wide shot of a palace room filled with games and painted boards

dialogue.text: The treasury did not stop at gods and postures. It turned to games and pastimes, recording boards and pieces, showing how a king who could not fight great wars still commanded a battlefield of leisure and intellect.

panels.shot: intimate medium shot of king and scribe in discussion at a desk

dialogue.text: To gather such variety, Mummadi needed more than artists. He drew on priests, artisans, yogis and scholars, weaving court knowledge into one organized palace book instead of many jealous, private memories.

panels.shot: slow tracking shot along shelves of manuscripts in a later archive

dialogue.text: Long after Mummadi was gone, the Sritattvanidhi lay in palace and institutional custody. When modern researchers opened its folios in Mysore’s Oriental Research Institute, they found a king’s mind arranged in pigments and script.

panels.shot: medium shot of a modern scholar studying the manuscript

dialogue.text: Norman Sjoman and others would later trace lines of yoga teaching through these painted bodies and annotations. The compendium, once a working palace manual, became a key to Mysore’s contribution to modern yoga history.

panels.shot: medium shot of Krishnaraja Wodeyar III listening to a court poet in a decorated hall

dialogue.text: Text alone still had its place. Under his patronage, Devachandra’s Rajavali Katha retold Mysore’s past in Kannada, stitching dynastic memory and legend into a court chronicle that later historians would carefully test and use.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of the king marking a passage in the chronicle

dialogue.speaker: krishnaraja_wodeyar_iii
dialogue.text: If our story is not written, others will write it for us.
Rajavali Katha did not give a neutral record; it gave a Mysore voice. In an age when colonial pens described his land, Mummadi made sure his court’s version also survived.

panels.shot: wide shot of Jagan Mohan Palace facade with artists and students entering

dialogue.text: Jagan Mohan Palace became more than a residence. It housed the ateliers and, later, collections that kept Mysore painting alive, with the Sritattvanidhi as silent tutor behind many a canvas.

panels.shot: introspective close-up on the king’s face in old age

dialogue.text: He could not recover the full sovereignty of his ancestors. Yet by arranging images and narratives, Mummadi shaped how Mysore would remember itself, long after imperial flags had changed above its fort.

panels.shot: composed split-scene showing palace past and archive present

dialogue.text: Today his illuminated volumes demand careful, critical reading; legend, prescription and history intertwined. Yet they remind us of a simple, enduring act — a ruler turning his court into a workshop to guard knowledge against forgetting.
